rationale: The reading is supported: the Queen tests the visitor's claim to be a real Princess. The quotation is not verbatim; the passage says "Ah! we shall soon see that!"
The watchman wants to examine "the little glimmering things somewhat nearer, especially the moon," which supports curiosity. The quotation is a paraphrase, not verbatim.
The flower keeps the maiden present in his mind, so the bond is supported. The quotation is not verbatim; the passage has her "peeping forth with her bright blue eyes."
"The small flame went out, the stove vanished" supports the idea of fragile, short-lived comfort. The quotation is not verbatim.

The collar does ignore the garter's repeated "Don't come so near me." But the narrator's explicit criticism targets its boasting ("that was not true... but he boasted"). The quotation is not verbatim.
"I am not fit for my good, profitable office... no one shall know anything about it" supports fear of being exposed as unfit. The quotation is not verbatim.
The quotation is verbatim, but the passage does not say her fondness is why she believes him. She is also flattered by the idea that she is cured, so the causal link is partly inferred.
The quotation is verbatim. The shoes are linked to the princess and to a count's child, so imitation of aristocratic fashion is directly supported.
The quotation is verbatim, but the animated details (trumpeters, rattling armor, talking flowers) make the house lively and welcoming. They do not mainly point to its decay.
The quotation is verbatim, and the passage does show beings serving her. But it says her power "lies in her heart, because she is a sweet and innocent child," which the reading leaves out.

The quotation is not verbatim; the passage says "Night stood still and mute." Night does delay the mother, but she asks out of fondness for the songs and then helps, so "cruelly" is only weakly supported.
The speech is ironic: it ends with the hope of being "boiled black, and laid on silver dishes." That undercuts a reading of plain affection. The quotation is not verbatim ("dowry and inheritance").
The quotation is verbatim. The ladies' objection ("we should not like that at all") and her appeal to her rank directly support the reading.
"Unperceived, he thrusts an arrow to their bosom" supports the reading that Cupid strikes without being welcomed. The quotation is a paraphrase.
The quotation is verbatim, and the Raven does tie her help to an expectation of future gratitude. "Conditioned" is slightly too strong, since the help is given before any gratitude is asked for.

Only the Corsor section stresses modern growth. The Roeskilde part celebrates ancient kings and history, so "chiefly modern" is only partly supported. The quotation is not verbatim ("just rising into importance").
The quotation is verbatim. The narrator's "What strange things... Selenites sometimes take into their heads!" directly mocks their self-centered certainty.
The quotation is verbatim, and the tree's fear for its splendor is clear. Later it also wants to take part ("Am I to do nothing whatever?"), so the reading is not the whole picture.
The quotation is verbatim, but the scene is satirical. Claims of birth are inflated or false, and a housedog judges the Leap-frog's family, so taking noble birth seriously misreads the tone.
The quotation is verbatim. "I must and will find the bell" and his going on "without being disheartened" strongly support the reading.
